In Ratlam the district cricket trials were on Sunday, and the coach had told Wasim, in front of everyone, that "your kind" never lasted in the team. Madhav heard about it at the tea stall and saw red. He was already planning the speech he would give the coach, the post he would write, the uncles he would call.

At home his sister Damini was folding clothes. "Did you ask Wasim what he wants?"

"He'll want me to fight for him."

"Will he? Or will he feel like a child who needs rescuing?"

Madhav went to Wasim's house that evening. "What do you want to do? I'm with you either way."

Wasim was quiet a long time. "I want to play on Sunday. If he says it again, I'll complain to the association myself. Just stand next to me."

On Sunday Madhav stood by the boundary rope. Wasim scored forty-two.

At the café in Stockholm where they both worked weekends, the new manager kept giving Jamal the back room and the dish pit, never the counter. On Tuesday he said to Jamal, loud enough to hear, "Customers prefer a more Swedish face at the front."

Anders felt heat rush up his neck. Before Jamal could answer, Anders stepped in. "That's discrimination. You can't say that. I'm reporting you."

On the walk home Jamal was silent. Finally he said, "You made it about you, man. I didn't get to say anything."

Anders stopped on the bridge. His first instinct was to defend himself. Instead he asked, "You're right. What do you want to do?"

"I want to write the complaint. In my words. You can sign as a witness."

They wrote it together that night at Jamal's kitchen table, Jamal typing, Anders reading over his shoulder only when asked.

First day, I told my friends, "Watch, he'll only favour his own people." I didn't know one thing about him. Only his name.

For a month I watched him like a detective, waiting to be right. Every small thing, I counted as proof.

Then my mother fell ill and I needed three days' leave in peak season. Yusuf bhai gave me five, and covered my machine himself. I felt so small. Not because he was kind. Because I'd been so sure.

That's when I started asking myself: this idea in my head, is it about this man, or about something I heard as a boy? You'll have ideas like that too. Everyone does. Notice them. Check them.

You asked why I sounded strange on the phone on Friday. Here's what happened. I was riding back from the library at 11:30, and a police jeep flashed its lights and waved me over near the flyover. My heart was pounding so hard I could hear it.

I remembered what Ammi always says. I switched off the scooter, took off my helmet slowly, and kept both hands on the handlebar. I said, "Good evening, sir. May I know why I've been stopped?" Trisha

I'm Maria, and I almost didn't report it. When my phone was snatched on the bus in Panaji, my first thought was: the police won't bother, they'll just laugh at me. Devika, my flatmate, said, "Try. What have you lost?"

So the next morning we went to the station with the phone's bill, my ID card, and the phone's number written down. I was nervous. The station was crowded and hot, and we waited for an hour. I kept my voice polite even when the constable at the desk sighed.

The officer who finally saw us wrote down everything. I asked, "May I have the complaint copy, stamped?" He gave me one.

The phone never came back. But with that copy I could block the SIM and claim the insurance. And I learned the station isn't as scary as I'd imagined.

Ritu came to me at 8 am in tears: her laptop had been stolen from the reading room overnight, with her whole thesis on it. She said, "There's no point going to the police. They never do anything for students."

Thursday night

I can't sleep. Today, reconciling accounts at the NGO, I found six invoices from a "vendor" whose address is our director's cousin's house. The amounts are large. The work was never done. I checked three times.

I'm Saurabh, I'm twenty-two, it's my first job, and I am terrified. If I say something and I'm wrong, I lose everything. If I'm right, maybe I lose everything anyway.

1. Copies of the invoices on a pen drive, kept at home, not on the office laptop.
2. Read the whistleblower policy in the employee handbook.
3. Call Nirmala di on Saturday. She works in a legal firm. Ask her about protections and the safest channel, maybe the board or the funder.

Then sleep.

Dear Vishal sir,

You were my manager at my first internship, and you once said I could write if things got hard. They have.

Three months ago I reported that our site supervisor was signing off safety checks without doing them. I told the compliance officer, who thanked me, met me twice, and has started an inquiry. I thought I'd done the right thing.

Since then my boss has taken me off the main project. Colleagues who used to share lunch now eat at another table. Nobody says it's because of the report, but I feel it every day, like being punished for telling the truth.

I've started writing down each change with the date, like you taught us to document everything. I've also joined a professional engineers' group that meets on Saturdays; two of them have been through this.

I don't regret it. But it's lonely. Could we talk on the phone this weekend?

Uday

qa.q: What was the site supervisor doing without checks?
qa.a: The site supervisor was signing off safety checks without doing them.

qa.q: How does Uday feel since the report?
qa.a: Uday feels punished and lonely, as if being made to pay for telling the truth, but does not regret it.

qa.q: What wise steps is Uday taking?
qa.a: Uday documents each change with dates, joins an outside professional group and reaches out to a trusted former manager.

qa.q: How might the colleagues who moved tables see Uday?
qa.a: They may fear being linked to the report or the boss's anger, so they keep their distance even if some agree with Uday.

grounding: The letter shows a young employee frozen out after reporting wrongdoing, documenting retaliation and leaning on outside support.
